title: Ten Things Leaders Can Do to Improve Teacher Morale in Early 2021
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Writing to school leaders in the depths of pandemic-era remote teaching, Dave Stuart Jr. argues that falling teacher morale is best addressed at the 'micro' level of individual relationships rather than macro policy fixes. He grounds his argument in his 'five key beliefs' framework — Value, Belonging, Effort, Efficacy, and Credibility — showing how each belief specifically erodes when teachers face prolonged hardship like 2020's disruptions. Stuart contends that periods of transition are unusually malleable for belief formation, comparing it to how a broken bone heals stronger if set properly, which makes this a moment of opportunity rather than just crisis management for leaders. The bulk of the article offers ten concrete, evidence-informed interventions leaders can run at staff meetings or one-on-ones, organized under each of the five beliefs, including moments of genuine connection, values-affirmation writing, and Stanford researcher Geoff Cohen's 'magic feedback' framing. Throughout, Stuart insists these are small, low-effort investments rather than heavy programmatic overhauls, aimed at leaders who want to unlock teacher motivation without adding to their own or their staff's workload.
points: Stuart frames teacher demoralization not as a macro policy problem but a micro, relational one, arguing leaders get more traction from person-level care than system-level fixes.

The core model is the 'five key beliefs' (Value, Belonging, Effort, Efficacy, Credibility); Stuart maps how each belief specifically erodes under crisis conditions like 2020's remote-teaching disruption.

Citing Geoff Cohen's Stanford research, Stuart highlights 'magic feedback' framing ('I have very high expectations, and I know you can reach them') as an especially effective belief-building intervention for boosting subsequent effort.
Ten concrete, low-lift interventions are organized by which belief they target, from staff MGCs (moments of genuine connection) for Credibility to values-affirmation writing exercises for Value.
Stuart's bone-healing metaphor argues that transition periods are unusually high-leverage for leaders: beliefs that are 'set properly' during a crisis emerge stronger than before, not just restored.
quotes: We teachers should be known for our love — for the degree to which we understand and care about the pains and concerns and triumphs and successes of all the folks in our society. After all, all the non-teachers we live with are or were our students or our students' parents.

In order to unlock the performance potential of teachers, you've got to seek remedy for this rising demoralization — not at the macro "fix the system" level, but at the micro "people in your actual life and on your actual team" level.

Motivation is the state in which I want to do something in the deepest parts of me. Way deeper than carrots, way deeper that sticks. My desire is for the thing I am motivated to do; my will is pointed toward it.
When a teacher knows those five things to be true, that is a teacher who will work hard and with joy, even amidst adversity. You don't have to incentivize her, you don't have to threaten her.
So here's the good news: there's lots that leaders can do, and its not hyper-heavy lifting. Small, wise investments in teacher motivation can compound over time into high teacher morale.

A team of researchers led by Stanford's Geoff Cohen analyzed the impact of various kinds of written feedback on student work, and they found that one type of feedback outpaced all the rest in improving subsequent effort.

One of the greatest misunderstandings around growth mindset is that if we can just convince people that their intelligence is incremental rather than innate, then they'll put forth more effort, and they'll succeed. The trouble here is simple: not all effort works.

Track attempted moments of genuine connection with each of your staff members. If you've got a smaller team, try to do one MGC per week for each member; for larger teams, shoot for biweekly or once a month.
